title: Why Difficult Students Need Responsibility
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that giving difficult students low-stakes classroom jobs can keep them occupied but doesn't actually change behavior; real transformation requires responsibilities with genuine stakes and the real possibility of failure. He critiques conventional 'self-esteem building' through false praise and external rewards, arguing self-esteem must arise from authentic accomplishment rather than being handed out. Counterintuitively, he claims that when the stakes are genuinely high, students are less likely to fail, because they take the trust seriously. If a student does fail, the response should simply be to follow the classroom management plan, hold them accountable, and give them another chance—reinforcing a durable, internally rooted sense of capability rather than a fragile, externally propped self-image.
points: Low-stakes classroom jobs keep difficult students occupied but don't produce lasting behavior change.
Real behavior change requires responsibilities with genuine stakes and a real possibility of failure.
'Building' self-esteem through false praise and external rewards is a misnomer—genuine self-esteem must come from authentic accomplishment.
Counterintuitively, when stakes are genuinely high, students are less likely to fail because they take the trust seriously.
If a student does fail at a high-stakes responsibility, follow the classroom management plan, hold them accountable, and give them another chance rather than writing them off.
quotes: It’s not uncommon for teachers to give their most challenging students classroom jobs and other mild responsibilities.
To change behavior there must be higher stakes involved. In other words, to make the strategy effective... failure must be a possibility.

Building up” self-esteem is often cited as a key to helping difficult students. But the idea as it's commonly interpreted and used... is a misnomer, because self-esteem isn't something that can be handed out, granted, or created from the outside.

Indeed, there is risk involved using this strategy. Asking them to lead the science experiment or be the designated speaker could end in disaster. But the surprising truth is, when the stakes are high, there is less chance they’ll mess it up.
Follow your classroom management plan, hold them accountable, and then get them right back up on the horse.
Giving them a chance to do something they didn’t know they could do, on the other hand, is a prescription for bona fide, long-term change in behavior and a healthy belief in their abilities.
